A Stokes line is produced when the photon **loses** energy to the molecule, so its
wavelength is **greater**.
**Step 1 — recall the Raman process.** An incident photon of energy hν₀ interacts with a
molecule and is scattered with a **changed** energy ✓
**Step 2 — take the Stokes case.** The molecule is left in a **higher** vibrational or
rotational state, so it takes energy **from** the photon:
hν_scattered = hν₀ − **ΔE** ✓
**Step 3 — convert to wavelength.** Lower energy means lower frequency, and since
λ = c/ν, a **longer** wavelength ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** Stokes lines have **wavelength greater than the original** ✓
**The companion case.** **Anti-Stokes** lines: the molecule is already **excited** and
gives energy **to** the photon ✓ so hν = hν₀ + ΔE and the wavelength is **shorter**.
**Why anti-Stokes lines are weaker.** They need the molecule to be excited **before** the
collision ✓ and at room temperature the Boltzmann factor e^(−ΔE/kT) makes such molecules
rare. The Stokes lines are therefore much the stronger, often by a factor of ten or more.
**The unshifted line.** Most photons scatter **elastically** - **Rayleigh** scattering -
with no change of wavelength ✓ Only about **one photon in 10⁶** is scattered inelastically,
which is why the Raman effect needed intense sources and long exposures until lasers
arrived.
**Why the shift is characteristic of the molecule.** ΔE is a **vibrational** energy
level spacing ✓ so the Raman shift, usually quoted in cm⁻¹, is a fingerprint. The
shifts are the same whatever the exciting wavelength - which distinguishes Raman lines
from fluorescence.
**A worked instance.** Excitation at 500 nm (20000 cm⁻¹) from a bond vibrating at
1000 cm⁻¹:
Stokes: 19000 cm⁻¹ = **526 nm** ✓
anti-Stokes: 21000 cm⁻¹ = **476 nm** ✓
placed symmetrically about the exciting line in **frequency**, though not in wavelength.
**The discovery.** **C. V. Raman** and K. S. Krishnan, Calcutta, **28 February 1928** ✓
using filtered sunlight and liquid benzene. Raman received the Nobel Prize in 1930 - the
first Asian to win it in a science - and the date is kept as India's National Science Day.
**Why Raman spectroscopy is valuable.** It identifies molecules **non-destructively**,
works through glass and water, and needs no sample preparation ✓ It is used in forensics,
pharmaceuticals, art conservation and - on Mars - by rover instruments.
**How it complements infrared spectroscopy.** IR requires a change in **dipole moment**;
Raman requires a change in **polarisability** ✓ Symmetric vibrations invisible in the
infrared often show strongly in the Raman spectrum.
∴ wavelength greater than that of the original line.

For a moving observer the apparent frequency is f(v + u)/v, and doubling it needs
**u = v**.
**Step 1 — write the Doppler formula for an approaching observer.**
f′ = **f(v + u)/v** ✓
**Step 2 — set f′ = 2f.**
2f = f(v + u)/v
2v = v + u ✓
**Step 3 — solve.**
**u = v** ✓ the observer must travel at the speed of sound.
**Why the observer's motion raises the pitch.** He meets the wavefronts **sooner** ✓
The wavelength in the medium is unchanged at λ = v/f, but he sweeps through them at the
relative speed v + u, so he encounters (v + u)/λ of them per second.
**Why the formula differs for a moving source.** A moving **source** compresses the
**wavelength** itself:
f′ = **fv/(v − u_s)** ✓ To double the frequency this way needs only u_s = **v/2** ✓ -
half as fast. The two cases are **not** symmetrical, because the medium provides a
preferred frame.
**That asymmetry is a real physical distinction.** With the source moving at v the
frequency becomes **infinite** - the sonic boom ✓ With the observer moving at v it is
merely doubled. No such asymmetry exists for light, where there is no medium and only
the **relative** velocity matters.
**A worked instance.** v = 340 m s⁻¹, f = 500 Hz, observer at 340 m s⁻¹:
f′ = 500(340 + 340)/340 = **1000 Hz** ✓ one octave higher - and the observer is flying at
Mach 1.
**What happens on receding.**
f′ = f(v − u)/v ✓ and at u = v the observer outruns the sound entirely: f′ = **0**, and
he hears nothing.
**Why the general formula is worth memorising as one expression.**
f′ = f(v ± u_o)/(v ∓ u_s) ✓ upper signs for approach, lower for recession - observer's
speed in the numerator, source's in the denominator.
**Everyday evidence.** The drop in pitch as an ambulance passes ✓ a **source** effect,
the frequency falling from fv/(v − u) to fv/(v + u) as it goes by.
**Where the Doppler effect is used.** Radar speed traps, weather radar, Doppler
echocardiography, and the **red shift** of galaxies ✓ Hubble's law rests on the optical
version of this formula.
**Reading the distractors.** **v/2** ✗ is the answer for a moving **source** - the
intended trap. **2v** ✗ and **3v** ✗ would give f′ = 3f and 4f ✓
∴ v.

A difference of **30 dB** means a factor of **10³** in intensity.
**Step 1 — write the decibel definition.**
L = **10 log₁₀(I/I₀)** ✓
**Step 2 — write it for the two sounds.**
60 = 10 log₁₀(I₁/I₀) → I₁/I₀ = **10⁶** ✓
30 = 10 log₁₀(I₂/I₀) → I₂/I₀ = **10³** ✓
**Step 3 — form the ratio.**
I₁/I₂ = 10⁶/10³
= **10³ = 1000** ✓
**The shortcut.** Subtract the levels first:
ΔL = 60 − 30 = **30 dB** ✓
ratio = 10^(ΔL/10) = 10³ = **1000** ✓
**Why the scale is logarithmic.** The ear responds to an enormous range - from
10⁻¹² W m⁻² at the threshold of hearing to 1 W m⁻² at the threshold of pain ✓ twelve
orders of magnitude. Compressing that into 0-120 dB makes the numbers manageable, and
matches the roughly logarithmic response of the ear itself.
**Useful decibel equivalents.**
**3 dB** → ratio **2** ✓
**10 dB** → ratio **10** ✓
**20 dB** → ratio **100** ✓
**30 dB** → ratio **1000** ✓
Each **10 dB** multiplies the intensity by ten.
**Why 1000 times the intensity does not sound 1000 times as loud.** Perceived loudness
roughly **doubles** for every 10 dB ✓ so a 60 dB sound seems about **eight** times as
loud as a 30 dB one, though it carries a thousand times the energy. This is the
**Weber-Fechner** relation at work.
**What these levels correspond to.** 30 dB is a **quiet library**; 60 dB is **ordinary
conversation** ✓ The gulf in physical intensity between them is far greater than the ear
suggests.
**The amplitude ratio.** Since I ∝ a²,
a₁/a₂ = √1000 = **31·6** ✓ a much smaller factor than the intensity ratio, and the reason
sound-pressure levels use 20 log₁₀ rather than 10 log₁₀.
**Why I₀ = 10⁻¹² W m⁻².** It is the nominal **threshold of hearing** at 1 kHz ✓ chosen so
that 0 dB marks the faintest audible sound.
**Reading the distractors.** **2** ✗ confuses the ratio of the **levels** (60/30) with the
ratio of intensities. **100** ✗ is a 20 dB difference, and **4** ✗ a 6 dB one ✓
Note: the printed key marks the second option, 2. That is the ratio of the decibel
**numbers**, not of the intensities. Since 10^(30/10) = 1000, the correct choice is the
first option, and the key has been corrected to it.
∴ 1000.

Intensity falls as **1/r²**, so amplitude falls as **1/r**.
**Step 1 — write the intensity law.** For a point source radiating uniformly,
I = **P/4πr²** ✓ the power spread over a sphere.
**Step 2 — relate intensity to amplitude.**
I ∝ **a²** ✓
**Step 3 — combine.**
a² ∝ 1/r², so **a ∝ 1/r** ✓
**Step 4 — form the ratio.**
a_P/a_Q = r_Q/r_P
= **9/4** ✓
**Why the amplitude falls more slowly than the intensity.** Intensity is the **square**
of amplitude ✓ The intensity ratio here is (9/4)² = **81/16**, far larger than the
amplitude ratio - which is why a sound that is barely audible still has an appreciable
pressure amplitude.
**Why the inverse-square law holds.** Energy is **conserved** and spreads over a sphere
of area 4πr² ✓ In a non-absorbing medium none is lost, so the power through every sphere
is the same and the intensity must fall as 1/r².
**Why "non-absorbing" matters.** Real air absorbs sound, the more so at **high**
frequencies ✓ With absorption the fall is faster than 1/r² - which is why distant thunder
is a low rumble: the high frequencies have been stripped out.
**The check in decibels.**
ΔL = 20 log₁₀(9/4) = 20(0·352) = **7·0 dB** ✓ so Q is 7 dB quieter than P - a clearly
audible difference.
**Where the law fails.** Close to a source larger than a wavelength, in the **near
field** ✓ and for **line** sources such as a busy road, where the intensity falls as
**1/r** and the amplitude as 1/√r. A motorway is therefore audible much further than a
point source of the same power.
**A worked instance.** A source of 1 W:
at 4 m: I = 1/(4π x 16) = **5·0 x 10⁻³ W m⁻²** ✓
at 9 m: I = 1/(4π x 81) = **9·8 x 10⁻⁴ W m⁻²** ✓
ratio **5·06 = 81/16** ✓ and the square root, 2·25 = 9/4, is the amplitude ratio.
**The same law elsewhere.** Light from a star, gravitational and electrostatic fields,
radiation dose from a point source ✓ all obey it, and for the same geometrical reason.
**Why this is used in practice.** Doubling the distance from a point source of noise
reduces the level by **6 dB** ✓ the basic rule of noise control.
**Reading the distractors.** **4/9** ✗ inverts the ratio - the nearer point must have the
**larger** amplitude. **3/2** ✗ and **2/3** ✗ take the square root of the distances
instead ✓
∴ 9/4.

Uniform force, start from rest: use **v² = 2as** with a = qE/m.
**Step 1 — find the force.**
F = qE = (3·2 x 10⁻¹⁹)(1·6 x 10⁵) ✓
= **5·12 x 10⁻¹⁴ N** ✓
**Step 2 — find the acceleration.**
a = F/m = 5·12 x 10⁻¹⁴/6·4 x 10⁻²⁷ ✓
= **8 x 10¹² m s⁻²** ✓
**Step 3 — apply v² = u² + 2as with u = 0.**
v² = 2(8 x 10¹²)(2 x 10⁻²) ✓
= **3·2 x 10¹¹** ✓
**Step 4 — take the root.**
v = √(3·2 x 10¹¹) = √(32 x 10¹⁰)
= **4√2 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹** ✓ (about 5·66 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹)
**The check by energy.** Work done = qEs = (5·12 x 10⁻¹⁴)(2 x 10⁻²) = **1·024 x 10⁻¹⁵ J** ✓
½mv² = ½(6·4 x 10⁻²⁷)(3·2 x 10¹¹) = **1·024 x 10⁻¹⁵ J** ✓ the same, as it must be.
**In electron-volts.** The potential difference traversed is
V = Es = (1·6 x 10⁵)(2 x 10⁻²) = **3200 V** ✓
and the alpha particle carries 2e, so it gains **6400 eV = 6·4 keV** ✓
1·024 x 10⁻¹⁵ J ÷ 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ = 6400 eV ✓ confirming the figure.
**Why the acceleration is so enormous.** 8 x 10¹² m s⁻² is **10¹² g** ✓ Gravity is utterly
negligible here, which is why it was not mentioned: the electric force exceeds the weight
by about twelve orders of magnitude.
**Why the charge is 3·2 x 10⁻¹⁹ C.** An alpha particle is a **helium nucleus** - two
protons and two neutrons - so its charge is **2e** ✓ and its mass about **4u** =
6·64 x 10⁻²⁷ kg, close to the value given.
**Why the motion is uniformly accelerated.** The field is **uniform**, so the force is
constant ✓ and the equations of motion for constant acceleration apply exactly.
**A relativistic check.** v/c = 5·66 x 10⁵/3 x 10⁸ = **0·0019** ✓ well under 1%, so the
non-relativistic treatment is amply justified.
**The time taken.**
t = v/a = 5·66 x 10⁵/8 x 10¹² = **7·1 x 10⁻⁸ s = 71 ns** ✓
**Why the formula v = √(2qV/m) is worth knowing.**
v = √(2 x 6400 x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹/6·4 x 10⁻²⁷) = **5·66 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹** ✓ a third route to the
same answer, and the standard expression for any particle accelerated through a p.d.
**Reading the distractors.** **8 x 10⁵** ✗ omits a factor of √2 somewhere; **16 x 10⁵** ✗
is twice that; **2√3 x 10⁵** ✗ matches no consistent slip ✓
∴ 4√2 × 10⁵ ms⁻¹.

Coherence means a **constant phase difference** maintained over time.
**Step 1 — state the definition.** Two sources are coherent if the phase difference
between the waves they emit stays **constant** ✓ - not necessarily zero, but unchanging.
**Step 2 — see why that is the essential condition.** The interference term is
2√(I₁I₂)**cos δ** ✓ If δ is constant, the term survives and fringes appear. If δ varies
randomly, ⟨cos δ⟩ = **0** and the fringes wash out.
**Step 3 — conclude.** **Having a constant phase difference** ✓
**Why equal wavelength is necessary but not sufficient.** Two independent sodium lamps
emit the same wavelength ✓ yet produce **no** fringes, because each atom radiates for
only about 10⁻⁸ s before its phase jumps at random. Equal wavelength alone is not
coherence.
**Why equal speed is beside the point.** In the same medium **all** light travels at the
same speed ✓ The condition is automatically satisfied and therefore distinguishes
nothing.
**Why the shape of the wavefront is irrelevant.** Spherical or plane, fringes form
provided the phase relation is fixed ✓ Young used spherical wavefronts from two
pinholes; Fresnel's biprism gives much the same result with a different geometry.
**Why equal amplitude is not required either.** Unequal amplitudes merely reduce the
**contrast**, leaving the dark fringes imperfectly dark ✓ The fringes still form, in the
same positions.
**How coherence is obtained in practice.** By splitting **one** wave in two ✓
**division of wavefront**: Young's slits, Fresnel's biprism, Lloyd's mirror
**division of amplitude**: thin films, Newton's rings, the Michelson interferometer
In every case the two beams share a common phase history, so their difference is fixed.
**The coherence time and length.**
τ_c ≈ **1/Δν**, and L_c = **cτ_c** ✓
A sodium lamp: Δν ≈ 5 x 10¹¹ Hz, so L_c ≈ **0·6 mm**. A stabilised laser: L_c of many
**kilometres**. The path difference must stay within L_c for fringes to be seen - which
is why white light, with L_c of a few micrometres, shows only a handful of fringes.
**Spatial versus temporal coherence.** **Temporal** coherence concerns the spectral
purity; **spatial** coherence concerns the phase relation **across** the beam ✓ Young's
experiment needs both, which is why the source slit S and a filter are traditionally
used.
**Why the laser transformed these experiments.** **Stimulated** emission forces all the
photons into one phase ✓ giving coherence lengths a million times a lamp's, and making
interferometry over long paths - gravitational-wave detection, for instance - possible.
∴ having a constant phase difference.

Diffraction is shown by **both** sound and light, so it cannot distinguish them - that
is the incorrect statement.
**Step 1 — test the first statement.** "A mechanical wave may or may not be
transverse" ✓ **Correct**: waves on a string are transverse, sound in air is
longitudinal, and ripples on water are a mixture of both.
**Step 2 — test the second.** "Mechanical waves cannot propagate in vacuum" ✓
**Correct**: they need a **medium** to carry the disturbance, which is why a bell in an
evacuated jar falls silent.
**Step 3 — test the third.** "Diffraction distinguishes sound from light" ✗
**Incorrect**: **both** diffract, being waves. The difference is only one of **scale** -
sound's metre wavelengths bend round everyday obstacles, light's half-micron
wavelengths do not noticeably.
**Step 4 — test the fourth.** "A longitudinal wave must be mechanical" ✓ **Correct**:
electromagnetic waves are necessarily **transverse**, so a longitudinal wave in the
syllabus's sense requires a medium that can be compressed.
**Step 5 — conclude.** The **third** statement is the incorrect one ✓
**What does distinguish sound from light.** **Polarisation** ✓ Light can be polarised;
sound in a fluid cannot, being longitudinal. Also light travels in **vacuum** and at
3 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹, against sound's 340 m s⁻¹ in air.
**Why the scale difference is so striking.** A 340 Hz note has λ = **1 m**, comparable
with a doorway, so it spreads through nearly 180° ✓ Visible light at 5 x 10⁻⁷ m
diffracts by about 10⁻⁴ rad at the same opening - invisible to the eye. One hears round
a corner but does not see round one, and the reason is wavelength, not any difference in
kind.
**How light's diffraction is demonstrated.** Make the obstacle **small enough** ✓ A slit
of a few micrometres, a fine grating, or the edge of a razor blade all produce clear
fringes - and the **Poisson spot** at the centre of a circular shadow settled the matter
in 1818.
**Why electromagnetic waves must be transverse.** Maxwell's equations in free space
require **∇·E = 0**, which forbids a component of E along the direction of
propagation ✓
**Why longitudinal waves need a medium.** The wave is a succession of **compressions and
rarefactions** of matter ✓ With nothing to compress, there is nothing to propagate -
hence no sound in space.
**The one subtlety.** **Plasma oscillations** and sound in solids can be longitudinal
and are still mechanical ✓ The fourth statement holds in every case met in the syllabus.
**How to attack such questions.** Test each statement **separately** against a known
example ✓ One counter-example is enough to condemn a statement; here, a diffraction
grating for light and an open doorway for sound dispose of the third.
∴ 'Diffraction' helps us to distinguish between sound wave and light wave.
